Boys and Cancer

Yes, it can happen to boys too. Let’s talk about it.

Facts, support, and respect

Why talk about this?

  • Cancer doesn’t check age or gender first
  • Boys and men often stay quiet about symptoms
  • Silence and myths make people wait longer for help
  • Knowing the facts helps us support each other

Can boys get cancer?

Yes. Cancer can affect anyone, including children and teenagers.

  • “Childhood cancer” means cancer in people aged 0 to 19
  • Common types: leukemia (blood cancer), brain tumors, lymphomas and bone cancers
  • It is rare, but real, and treatment works for many
  • Where good care is available, about 85% of children with cancer survive

What is cancer?

  • Body cells normally grow, divide and die in an orderly way
  • In cancer, some cells grow out of control and can form a lump called a tumor
  • Some cancers can spread to other parts of the body
  • You cannot catch it from someone. It is not contagious

Can boys get breast cancer?

Yes. It’s rare, but it’s real.

  • Boys and men have breast tissue too
  • Less than 1% of all breast cancers happen in men
  • In the US, about 1 in 833 men will have it in their lifetime
  • Risk rises with age, so it is extremely rare in boys and teens, but anyone can notice a change and should speak up

The wake-up call

“Wait… that can happen to us too?!”

  • Many boys think breast cancer is only a women’s disease
  • That belief is exactly why men find it late
  • Learning the truth early can save lives

Signs to watch for

  • A lump or thickening in the chest, often painless
  • Nipple discharge, or a nipple that turns inward
  • Dimpling, redness or flaky skin on the chest
  • Sores on the nipple, or swollen lymph nodes under the arm

Most lumps are not cancer, but always get them checked by a doctor.

Why it gets missed

  • “That’s a women’s thing,” so nobody looks
  • Embarrassment keeps boys and men from speaking up
  • Men are more likely than women to put off seeing a doctor
  • So it’s often found later, when it’s harder to treat

Caught early, five-year survival is above 95%.

“Boys can’t get that.”

  • Myth: Cancer only happens to girls and women. Fact: It can affect anyone.
  • Myth: Talking about it is weak. Fact: Speaking up early is brave.
  • Myth: You can catch it from a friend. Fact: Cancer is not contagious.

Joking about it or dismissing it keeps people silent. Don’t be that person.

Treatment: what to expect

  • Common treatments: surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, hormone and targeted therapy
  • Men with breast cancer are treated much like women are
  • Side effects can include tiredness, hair loss, nausea and mood changes
  • Treatment is long, and some days are harder than others
  • At the same stage, survival is about the same for men and women

How to support a boy with cancer

  • Treat him like himself. He is still the same person
  • Visit, message, call, even when it feels awkward
  • Be specific: “Can I bring you the notes?” beats “Let me know if you need anything”
  • Let him decide what he can do, and be fine with plans changing
  • Include him. Loneliness hurts too

Helping a friend or family member, respectfully

  • Listen more than you talk
  • Ask before sharing his news with anyone
  • Respect his privacy: his health, his story
  • Offer practical help: rides, meals, homework, chores
  • Look after yourself too. Talk to a trusted adult

What to say, and what to avoid

Say

  • “I’m here for you.”
  • “Want to hang out, or just talk?”
  • “I don’t know what to say, but I care.”

Avoid

  • “You’ll be fine.”
  • “Everything happens for a reason.”
  • “What did you do to get it?”

Where to find help

  • A doctor, school nurse or clinic, for any symptom or worry
  • American Cancer Society: cancer.org
  • KidsHealth (teens section): kidshealth.org
  • CDC: cdc.gov/breast-cancer

Boys can get cancer. Speak up, check in, show up.

Thank you!
